content:
Aisha bint Abu Bakr is the wife of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about whom the most questions are asked, and most of the questions come from one report. She was the daughter of Abu Bakr, the first caliph, and she lived nearly fifty years after the death of the Prophet.

This article takes five of the questions in turn, gives the sources, and says where the evidence is disputed. It should be read with the rest of her record, which is long.

The best-known report, in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, is from Aisha herself: that she was married at six and the marriage was consummated at nine, after the migration to Medina.[1] The sources state it without qualification, and nothing in the classical literature softens it. Most classical scholars accepted it, and it is the view stated in most books.

Some modern scholars question it, on the grounds that other reports point to an older age. One argument compares her age with that of her sister Asma, who by the biographical dictionaries was about ten years older and died at 100 in 73 AH. That would make Aisha about seventeen or eighteen at the time of the marriage.[2] Others point to reports that she took part in the battle of Uhud as a water carrier, in a battle from which the Prophet is also reported to have sent back boys under fifteen.[3] A third line of criticism notes that the best-known version passes through Hisham ibn Urwa, whom the biographical sources call reliable. Ibn Hajar, in his Tahdhib, quotes Yaqub ibn Shayba that nothing was held against him until he moved to Iraq, where he narrated more freely from his father, and that the people of his own town objected to this.[4]

The report in Bukhari is stronger by chain, and Muslim scholars through the centuries took it at face value; the arguments against it are about internal consistency of the dates. The question is open among serious scholars. Both positions are argued from Muslim sources.

A separate objection, heard often online, is that consummation at nine is not a dating dispute but a biological impossibility: that no girl at that age is physically capable of what the report describes. This claim is false as stated. Early puberty, with menarche well below nine, is a recognised clinical category rather than a theoretical one. Standard paediatric endocrinology defines precocious puberty as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age eight in girls, with menarche before nine and a half years counted as precocious rather than impossible.[18] Published case reports document menarche at six years old, and one documented case of full idiopathic precocious puberty, menarche included, presenting at six months of age.[19] Population studies that are not restricted to clinical cases find the same pattern at the edge of the normal range: in a stratified sample of nearly 20,000 girls in Bosnia and Herzegovina, three percent reached menarche before roughly eleven years old; in a clinical reference sample in the United States, the third percentile for non-Hispanic white girls fell at about ten years and eight months.[20] Nine years old sits just beyond that lower tail, in the range paediatric medicine already has a name for, not outside what a human body can do.

A related label sometimes attached to this marriage is clinical, not historical: pedophilia. The term has a fixed psychiatric definition, and it does not fit a single marriage lasting decades. The DSM-5 defines pedophilic disorder as recurrent, intense sexually arousing fantasies, urges or behaviors involving prepubescent children, persisting for at least six months, in a person at least 16 years old and at least five years older than the child.[21] The diagnosis describes a standing pattern of attraction to children as a class, not a single marriage within a 23-year run of marriages mostly to widows and divorcees, nor a marriage that continued, by every account, after Aisha had passed out of childhood and into her role as the Prophet's closest companion and, afterward, as a scholar and public figure for five more decades. Applying a clinical label built around a repeated pattern to one relationship, decades after the fact, is not a diagnosis; it is a word borrowed for its shock value.

In seventh-century Arabia, as in most of the world before the modern age, marriages were arranged by families, often at young ages, and the sources give no sign that her contemporaries found it remarkable. Quraysh attacked the Prophet for many things, including calling him a poet and a madman, and none of the reports record an attack on this marriage.

This is a point about the historical record. It is not a case that the practice is right now. The classical jurists generally allowed a father to give a minor daughter in marriage, held that the marriage was not to be consummated until she was physically able, and in some schools gave her an option to confirm or end it on reaching maturity. The Prophet's own saying is that a virgin is not to be married until her permission is sought.[5]

Modern Muslim states have mostly set a minimum age. Egypt and Tunisia set a minimum marriage age of 18, and Turkey sets 17, with a judge able to allow 16, with some exceptions, and most contemporary scholars support such limits for the protection of girls.[6] A small minority still cite the classical rules. The sources record how the marriage was seen in her day, and they leave the present question to be answered by the principles of the law.

The practice was not confined to seventh-century Arabia. Isabella of Valois was six years old when she married Richard II of England in 1396, a dynastic match sealing a peace treaty with France; the marriage contract itself deferred consummation until she turned twelve.[23] In British India in 1883, Mrinalini Devi was about nine or ten when she married the poet Rabindranath Tagore, then twenty-two; the marriage is recorded without any suggestion, from her biographers or his, that it was considered scandalous at the time.[24] Child marriage of this kind was legally unremarkable across much of the world into the twentieth century; treating a seventh-century Arabian marriage as a moral outlier, rather than an instance of a near-universal pre-modern pattern, reads the past by standards it did not share.

The record shows a woman with strong views and a place in public life. She argued with the Prophet and with the Companions. When the Quran later gave the wives a choice between worldly life and staying with him, she was the first to be asked and chose him.[7]

She also corrected senior Companions. When Masruq asked whether Muhammad had seen his Lord, she answered that whoever said so had lied, and cited the Quran's words that no vision can grasp God; Ibn Abbas took a different view, and both opinions were preserved.[8] The scholar al-Zarkashi collected her corrections of other Companions in a book, al-Ijāba.[9]

Her voice carried into politics. In 656 she travelled to Basra with Talha and al-Zubayr to press for justice for the murdered caliph Uthman, and the forces met Ali at the Battle of the Camel, where hers were defeated. Later sources report that she regretted the journey.[10] The tradition keeps both her action and her regret in the record.

She is credited with 2,210 hadith, one of the largest bodies from any Companion, and senior Companions came to her on matters of law, especially on the Prophet's private life, the rules of purity and the details of prayer, which only his family knew.[11] Abu Musa al-Ashari is reported to have said that whenever the Companions were unsure about a hadith, they asked Aisha and found that she had knowledge of it.[12]

After his death she taught men and women from her room, with a screen for those who needed it. Her pupil Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, her nephew, and through him much of the school of Medina, preserved her opinions. Another pupil, her grand-nephew al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, was counted with Urwa among the seven jurists of Medina. Women also studied under her, and her pupil Amra bint Abd al-Rahman became a leading transmitter in her own right. She died in Medina in 58 AH.

None of this fits a woman left timid or diminished by her marriage. In 36 AH she raised an army and rode at its head against the fourth caliph, Ali ibn Abi Talib, at the Battle of the Camel near Basra, a fight she lost and from which she later said she wished she had stayed home.[22] Whatever judgment is made of that decision, it is not the record of a woman without a voice.

In 627, on the return from a raid against the Banu Mustaliq, she was left behind by accident while looking for a lost necklace and brought back to the army by a Companion, Safwan.[13] Some in Medina spread a rumour, led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The Prophet waited a month, without revelation, before the Quran spoke: "Those who brought the lie are a group among you."[14] Ten verses clear her and warn the community against slander.[15]

The passage asks why believing men and women, on hearing the charge, did not think well of their own. The rumour also cost Abu Bakr personally: he had supported a poor relative, Mistah, who was among those who spread it, and he swore to stop that support. The Quran urged forgiveness, and Abu Bakr resumed his support.[16]

The same passage gave the law that a charge of adultery needs four witnesses, and a false charge is flogged.[17] The rule protects a woman's reputation from an unproved accusation. In the reports, Aisha had no witnesses to call, and her innocence was declared by revelation.

The bottom line

The sources say what they say about her age: the best-attested report puts the marriage at six and its consummation at nine, and Muslim scholars through the centuries accepted it. A minority of modern scholars argue for a later age from other reports in the same literature. Neither position should be softened or hidden, and neither claims that the practice is a model for today.

The larger part of the record concerns what she did. She was a jurist who was consulted by the senior Companions, a teacher of the next generation, a critic of her elders, and a woman whose honour was defended by the Quran itself. A fair judgement of her rests on all of that, and the single question of her age takes its place within it.

Notes

  1. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, the chapter on the Prophet's marriage to Aisha and her arrival in Medina; Sahih Muslim, Book of Marriage. Sahih al-Bukhari 3894, 5133 and 5158 (numbering as on sunnah.com); Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 7, p. 223, vol. 9, p. 190 and vol. 9, p. 224 (Shamela text).
  2. The ten-year age gap between Asma and Aisha is reported by Ibn Kathir and Ibn Asakir; Ibn Hajar, Taqrib al-tahdhib, gives Asma's death at 100 years old in 73 or 74 AH, citing Abu Nu'aym. Working back from that figure to Aisha's age at the Hijra is a modern argument, not a classical one; al-Dhahabi, in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', gives a wider gap of thirteen to nineteen years between the sisters, which would put Aisha younger than the seventeen-to-eighteen figure rests on. The age-gap figure itself traces to a single narrator, Abu'l-Zinad, whose own second report rounds it to roughly ten years rather than stating it exactly.
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari, a report of Anas on Aisha and Umm Sulaym carrying water skins at Uhud; its implications for her age are disputed. The report of Ibn Umar being sent back at Uhud at fourteen is also in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the Book of Testimonies. Sahih al-Bukhari 2880 (Anas on Aisha and Umm Sulaym at Uhud), Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 78 (Shamela text); Sahih al-Bukhari 2664 (Ibn Umar, Book of Witnesses, chapter on boys attaining puberty and their testimony), vol. 5, p. 276 (Shamela text; numbering as on sunnah.com).
  4. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Tahdhib al-Tahdhib (Risala edition), vol. 4, p. 275, the entry on Hisham ibn Urwa, with the verdicts of Ibn Sad, al-Ijli, Abu Hatim and Yaqub ibn Shayba, and the remark of Ibn Khirash on Malik (Shamela text).
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, the chapter on a virgin not being married until she consents. Sahih al-Bukhari 5136 (Book of Wedlock, "The father or the guardian cannot give a virgin or matron in marriage without her consent"), numbering as on sunnah.com.
  6. Egypt Child Law of 2008; the minimum age of 18 is also in the laws of Tunisia and Turkey (with a court exception in Turkey). The conditions of maturity and consent are in the classical law of marriage.
  7. Quran 33:28–29; Sahih al-Bukhari.
  8. Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, on whether the Prophet saw his Lord; Quran 6:103. Sahih Muslim 177a (sunnah.com numbering), the report of Masruq from Aisha.
  9. Al-Zarkashi, al-Ijāba li-īrād mā istadrakathu ʿĀʾisha ʿalā al-ṣaḥāba.
  10. Al-Tabari, Tarikh, on the Battle of the Camel; the reports of her regret are in the later biographical literature.
  11. Counts in the classical hadith literature; about 2,210.
  12. Jami al-Tirmidhi, Book of Virtues, on the virtues of Aisha. Jami al-Tirmidhi 3883 (Chapters on Virtues, the virtue of Aisha), graded hasan (Darussalam) on sunnah.com.
  13. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, the account of the slander (ifk). Sahih al-Bukhari 4141 (Military Expeditions, the narration of al-Ifk), numbering as on sunnah.com.
  14. Quran 24:11.
  15. Quran 24:11–20.
  16. Quran 24:22.
  17. Quran 24:4.
  18. Precocious puberty is defined as onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls, with menarche before 9.5 years classed as precocious. See the clinical definition in Vijayakumar, Fish and Diamond, "Precocious Puberty: Perspectives on Diagnosis and Management," Indian Journal of Pediatrics 81, no. 10 (2014): 1049-1056.
  19. Nienaber and van der Walt, "True Idiopathic Precocious Puberty Presenting at Six Months of Age: A Case Report," European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology 39, no. 1 (1991): 69-72; Banu et al. on menarche at age 6 associated with juvenile hypothyroidism, Mymensingh Medical Journal 23, no. 1 (2014): 180-183; a further case of precocious puberty presenting with menarche at age 6 is reported in BMJ Case Reports (2014), PMID 25178615.
  20. Catto-Smith et al. and Biro et al. report US clinical reference percentiles for age at menarche by ethnicity, with the 3rd percentile for non-Hispanic white girls at approximately 10 years 8 months; a stratified population study of 19,803 girls in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina found roughly 3 percent reaching menarche before approximately 11.04 years using probit analysis.
  21. American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed. (DSM-5), criteria for Pedophilic Disorder (302.2).
  22. Al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wal-Muluk, account of the Battle of the Camel (36 AH); the report of Aisha's later regret is widely transmitted in the historical sources on the battle.
  23. Isabella of Valois (1389-1409); the 1396 marriage and its consummation clause are recorded in the English and French chronicle sources for the Anglo-French peace of that year.
  24. Mrinalini Devi (c.1873-1902), married Rabindranath Tagore on 9 December 1883; her age at marriage is given as nine or ten across her biographers.
